subject: humanities
passage: Historical dictionaries date each word by the earliest written use their editors can find. As huge collections of old newspapers, letters, and pamphlets have been digitized and made searchable, editors have repeatedly found uses of familiar words decades older than the dates previously given in their entries. Lexicographer Tendai Moyo points out that a word must already be in use before anyone writes it down, and that a newly discovered document can reveal a use older than a word's recorded date but can never show that the word first appeared later than a text already found. It follows that, as more archives are searched, the recorded first dates of words ______
stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: will tend to move earlier or else remain unchanged.
choices.B: will be accurate for words found in newspapers but not for those in letters.
choices.C: will eventually match the dates on which the words were first spoken.
choices.D: will tend to move later as more documents come to light.

explanation.why: Moyo makes two points. A newly found document can push a word's first recorded date earlier, but it cannot push it later, since the older text already found still exists. Searching more archives can therefore only move dates earlier or leave them where they are.
explanation.A: Correct. New documents can only reveal earlier uses, never later ones, so recorded dates can only move earlier or stay the same.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text does not compare the accuracy of dates from newspapers with dates from letters.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Since words are in use before anyone writes them down, written records may never reach the date a word was first spoken.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This reverses Moyo's point that a new document can never show a word appeared later than a text already found.
